claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a disordered, single-phase bcc structure in superconducting high-entropy alloys.
The entropy-stabilized disordered bcc structure produces a robust, homogenized electronic band structure.
This electronic environment preserves strong electron–phonon coupling under extreme compression.
Preservation of the electronic environment and electron–phonon coupling makes superconductivity unusually resilient to pressure.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 is a superconducting high-entropy alloy.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 crystallizes in a bcc structure at ambient pressure.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 is a well-characterized single-phase material.
(TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 has an ambient-pressure Tc of approximately 7.8 K.
The alloy can be subjected to hydrostatic pressures approaching 200 GPa while retaining the bcc phase.
The cited alloy retains its bcc structure without a structural phase transition up to approximately 96 GPa.
The disordered bcc lattice promotes a uniform electronic density.
The disordered bcc lattice promotes robust electron–phonon interactions.
Chemical and structural disorder prevents dramatic changes in electronic structure during lattice compression.
Under increasing pressure, the Tc of (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 should continuously increase or form a plateau.
The Tc of (TaNb)0.67(HfZrTi)0.33 continuously increases up to 96 GPa.
Pure Nb and Ta typically show decreasing Tc under pressure.
The pressure dependence of Tc in the HEA is distinct from that of elemental Nb and Ta.
The proposed mechanism is limited to chemically well-mixed, disordered, primarily bcc high-entropy superconductors without pressure-induced structural transitions or significant magnetic scattering.
Minor compositional fluctuations, secondary phases, electron count, and disorder may independently influence the pressure dependence of Tc.
A pressure-induced Tc decrease resembling Nb or Ta would falsify the proposed pressure-resilience hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly excludes pressures that induce a structural phase transition, but the falsification rule treats an abrupt change concurrent with such a transition as falsifying the mechanism. A phase transition would instead place the observation outside the stated domain.
